1:
Which house was dedicated is the standing question. Matthew Henry starts from the custom: the pious Jews dedicated a new house to God, as at Deuteronomy 20:5, and David did so, royal palaces needing God’s protection as much as ordinary ones. Some conjecture, he adds, a re-dedication after Absalom had defiled it. Adam Clarke lays out the field: Solomon’s temple, the second temple under Zerubbabel, a third in the days of the Messiah, or the house David built on Zion. He notes that the word David in the title attaches not to the house but to the psalm, and follows Calmet in referring it to the place built on Araunah’s threshing floor after the plague — all the parts of the psalm, he says, agree to this. He reads the healing of the second verse accordingly: thou hast removed the plague by which my people were perishing in thousands before my eyes.

John Calvin keeps it a private house, since the title expressly names David, and dismisses two suppositions. That David was seized with heavy sickness when about to dedicate his palace is founded on no solid reason, and to restrict to sickness what is spoken generally of danger is likewise groundless. He thinks it more probable that with Absalom dead and his faction extinguished, David celebrated the divine favour as one returned from exile. Keil and Delitzsch defend David’s authorship against Hitzig, who finds Jeremiah’s hand everywhere: the parallels in Jeremiah are echoes of the psalms. They take it for David, come to the verge of the grave in the midst of his power, praising the Lord and calling the pious to join him.

The verb of the opening line is examined closely. Charles Ellicott notes that the Hebrew seems to mean to dangle, and so may be used of letting down or of drawing up; the cognate noun means a bucket, used at Exodus 2:19 of drawing water from a well. Here it is a metaphor of restoration from sickness, and does not refer to the incident in Jeremiah’s life, where a different word is used. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point against Hitzig: the word need not be explained of a lowering into a tank or dungeon, being a metaphor for raising up out of the depths of affliction. C.H. Spurgeon hears the antithesis — I will exalt thee, for thou hast exalted me — and calls the praise reasonable, the psalmist having been drawn up like a prisoner from a dungeon, like Joseph out of the pit. The last clause names the judgment David most feared of the three, having said let me fall into the hand of the Lord and not into the hand of man. John Gill takes extolling as declaring God to be what he is, the most High, who cannot be higher.

The deliverance itself is read at two depths. John Gill allows the plain sense, that his life being in danger was near the grave, but prefers to render it from hell, meaning horrors of conscience that were as hell itself to him. Charles Ellicott corrects the text instead: the received reading of the closing clause is considered ungrammatical by modern scholars, and the ordinary reading, kept by the Greek and Latin, means from those going down to the pit — that is, from the dead.

Augustine of Hippo makes the dedication another thing entirely. The psalm is of the joy of the resurrection and the renewing of the body to an immortal state, and not of the Lord only but of the whole church: in the psalm before, the tabernacle was finished in which we dwell in the time of war; now the house is dedicated which will abide in peace everlasting. It is whole Christ who speaks: where the psalm says thou hast healed me, he hears one who no longer bears a body enfeebled by mortality.
4:
Who the saints are that must sing they answer differently. Adam Clarke, holding to his reading of the occasion, takes them for the priests who wait upon God in his sanctuary, and calls them to magnify him for the mercy shown in staying the plague. C.H. Spurgeon takes them for the people of God at large: the psalmist could not praise God enough by himself and so enlisted the hearts of others, and would not fill his choir with reprobates but with sanctified persons who could sing from their hearts. If sinners are wickedly silent, let your holiness constrain you to sing. John Gill defines them from the word itself, which takes in those to whom God has been gracious, who are holy and godly persons, and who are kind and bountiful to others. Charles Ellicott adjusts the rendering, preferring play to Jehovah, ye saints of his, and for the second clause sing praises to his holy name, possibly with Exodus 3:15 in the poet’s mind.

On giving thanks at the remembrance of holiness, Adam Clarke turns polemical. He who can give thanks at that remembrance loves holiness and hates sin, seeing in it the holy nature he is to share. But most who call themselves Christians, he says, hate the doctrine of holiness and never hear it inculcated without pain, the principal part of their studies and their pastors’ being to find out with how little holiness they can rationally expect to enter the kingdom of God — a delusion he asks how long a holy God will suffer to pollute his church. C.H. Spurgeon handles the phrase gently: holiness inspires the deepest awe, yet the song of the seraphim is to be joined not dolefully, as though we trembled at it, but cheerfully.

The verse about anger parts them most sharply. John Gill denies that anger belongs to God at all. He is a simple, uncompounded, immovable and unchangeable being, and anger is never towards his people in reality but only in their apprehension, since he does those things which resemble what men do when they are angry. He turns away and hides his face, he chides and chastises, and then they conclude he is angry; when he returns and manifests his pardoning love, they understand that his anger is turned away. In that improper sense it is but for a moment.

Adam Clarke lets the Hebrew stand, admiring an elegant abruptness: for a moment in his anger; lives in his favour; in the evening weeping may lodge, but in the morning exultation. So good is God, he says, that he cannot delight in the ruin of his creatures; he afflicts that we may be partakers of his holiness. If he is angry it is but for a moment, and when we seek his face his favour is soon obtained — and there are lives in that favour, the life that now is and the life that is to come. This account of God’s slowness to anger, he adds, comes from a man long and deeply acquainted with him both as Judge and as Father.

Charles Ellicott renders the verse as four abrupt lines and draws out the picture behind them, which he calls thoroughly Oriental. Sorrow is the wayfarer who comes to the tent for a night’s lodging; but the metaphor is not carried on into his taking leave, and instead we have the sudden waking with a cry of joy, sudden as the Eastern dawn, without twilight or preparation. Never, he says, was faith in the divine love more beautifully expressed. John Wesley says only that the joy comes speedily and in season. C.H. Spurgeon grounds it in providence: the anger meant is those dispensations which are the chastisement ordered in God’s paternal government towards his erring children, such as the plague that fell upon Jerusalem for David’s sins — short judgments, and soon removed.
6:
Matthew Henry reads these verses as the first of three states David passed through, and the one in which we may see what we are too apt to be. He had long enjoyed prosperity and grew over-confident of its continuance: in health of body and given rest from his enemies, he never thought of having his body distempered or his government disturbed, and such was his interest in the hearts of his people that he thought his prosperity fixed like a mountain. Yet Henry notes that David ascribes it not to his own wisdom but to the divine goodness, and marks the word he chooses: he does not call it his heaven, as worldly people do who make their prosperity their felicity, but only his mountain — earth still, raised a little higher than the common level.

C.H. Spurgeon presses the danger of the calm. When all his foes were quiet and his rebellious son dead and buried, that was the time of peril, for many a vessel founders in a calm and no temptation is so bad as tranquillity. He rebukes the boast directly: David said more than was wise to say or even to think, since God has founded the world upon the floods to show us what a mutable, inconstant world it is, and unhappy is the man who builds on it, for he builds a dungeon for his hopes. As in a wheel the uppermost spokes descend to the bottom in due course, so it is with mortal conditions: many in the dust today shall be elevated tomorrow, while those now aloft shall soon grind the earth. Prosperity had turned the psalmist’s head, and the reader should beware lest the fumes of success get into his brain too.

Adam Clarke names the act the boast produced. Peace and prosperity had seduced David’s heart and led him to suppose his dominion so strong that adversity could never touch it; he wished to know the physical and political strength of his kingdom, and, forgetting to depend on God, desired Joab to number the people, which God punished as related at 2 Samuel 24:1, and which David here appears to acknowledge. Of the hidden face he adds that God showed himself displeased for that pride, and David found how vainly he had trusted in an arm of flesh. John Gill allows the prosperity to be either outward, when David was settled in his kingdom and at rest from his enemies, or inward and spiritual, when he was in the lively exercise of grace and favoured with communion with God.

What the mountain stands for divides them. John Wesley makes it the kingdom, kingdoms being usually called mountains in prophecy. Charles Ellicott reports that the reading varies — to my mountain, to my honour in the Greek, Latin and Syriac, or on mountains — but says the sense is the same: the mountain of strength, perhaps a mountain fortress, is an image of secure retreat, and doubtless Mount Zion was in the poet’s thought. John Gill turns it inward: as the church is compared to a mountain, so the soul of a child of God may be called his mountain, made strong by the Lord as to its state in Christ, being set on him, the Rock of ages. He adds that David found himself mistaken and acknowledges it: neither his prosperity nor its continuance was owing to his own goodness or strength.

Charles Ellicott attends throughout to how the thing is said. The opening pronoun is emphatic, so the line runs but as for me; prosperity is better rendered security, and the boast I shall never waver. The mental struggle by which the psalmist won his way to this faith is told most vividly, the very soliloquy being recalled, and the fluctuation of feeling is shown by the rapid succession of clauses without connecting conjunctions.
8:
The turn to prayer is noticed as a turn. John Gill observes that when the Lord had hid his face David was not stupid and unaffected, nor did he turn his back and seek to others, but cried after a departing God — which showed love and some degree of faith, looking again toward his holy temple and waiting until he returned. C.H. Spurgeon makes the same point a rule: prayer is the unfailing resource of God’s people, and when an earthquake makes our mountain tremble the throne of grace still stands firm. The hand which wounds can heal, so let us turn to him who smites us; and prayer is better solace than Cain’s building a city or Saul’s seeking for music, since mirth and carnal amusements are a sorry prescription for a mind distracted and despairing, while prayer will succeed where all else fails. Adam Clarke ties it again to the history: David found no help but in him against whom he had sinned, his confession being recorded at 2 Samuel 24:17; to make supplication is to continue urging the suit. Charles Ellicott would keep the verbs future rather than turning them into preterites, and begin the quotation here, so that the line runs as Symmachus has it, then I said, I will cry to thee, O Lord — the very words of what he calls this utter agony of prayer being given.

C.H. Spurgeon describes the shape of what follows. It was an argument with God, an urging of reasons, a pleading of his cause; not a statement of doctrinal opinions, nor a narration of experience, much less a sly hit at other people under pretence of praying — though all these and worse have been substituted for holy supplication at certain prayer-meetings. He wrestled with the angel of the covenant and therefore prevailed, head and heart, judgment and affections all at work to spread the case aright before the Lord of love. Spurgeon then puts the plea in his own words: wilt thou not lose a songster from thy choir, and one who loves to magnify thee; will there not be one witness the less to thy faithfulness and veracity? Adam Clarke and John Wesley read it the same way, that his being cut off will not magnify God’s mercy and that the question is simply what God would gain by it.

Charles Ellicott makes the loss God’s in a stronger sense. Death breaks the covenant relation between Israel and Jehovah and so causes loss to him as well as to them, since the grave has its own king or shepherd and death puts an end to all religious service; he compares Hezekiah’s song at Isaiah 38:18. And he states plainly what he thinks the argument presupposes: as yet no hope, not even a dim one, had arisen of praising God beyond the grave, the vision of the New Jerusalem with its countless throngs of the redeemed being still for the future.

John Gill answers a different question altogether, and at length. Death, he says, is not profitable to a man himself by way of merit: it does not atone for sin or merit heaven, and even the death of martyrs is not meritorious, since there is profit in no blood but the blood of Christ, by which peace is made and redemption obtained. Death is indeed consequentially profitable to good men, being an outlet of all sorrows and the inlet of joy, the saint’s passage to heaven. Nor is there profit in the blood of the saints to those who shed it, for when inquisition is made for it vengeance will be taken. Of the plea that follows he says only that it asks God to lift the light of his countenance again, to apply his pardoning grace and to deliver out of all afflictions.
11:
The answer to the prayer is registered as a sudden change. John Gill lists the mournings it may end — over sin, over afflictions, over spiritual decays, under Satan’s temptations, or, as here, because of the hidings of God’s face — and says the exchange comes when the Lord discovers his pardoning love, revives his work in the soul and takes off his afflicting hand. Charles Ellicott notes that the verse gives the answer to the prayer, and explains the pairing: mourning is literally beating the breast, so dancing forms a proper parallelism, though by another derivation the word would suggest piping. Adam Clarke prefers that second reading — turned my mourning into piping — and reads the verse from the history: I have not prayed in vain, and though I deserved to be cut off thou hast spared me and the remnant of my people, taking away the sackcloth when thou didst say to the destroying angel over Jerusalem, it is enough, stay now thy hand, as at 2 Samuel 24:16. John Wesley glosses the sackcloth as the garment worn in mourning, as at Esther 4:1, and the girding as joy surrounding him like a garment.

C.H. Spurgeon dwells on what is given in exchange. God takes away the mourning of his people and gives not quiet only but a great deal more, making their hearts dance at the sound of his name. He takes off the sackcloth, a delight in itself, but then clothes us, and not with any common dress but with that royal vestment which is the array of glorified spirits in heaven. Many a poor man wears this apparel wrapped about his heart though fustian and corduroy are his only outward garb, and need not envy the emperor in all his pomp.

What the glory is that sings divides the last verse. Charles Ellicott reports that the possessive is wanting in the Hebrew and in all the older versions except the Greek and Latin; the Chaldee makes the word concrete and renders it the nobles, while the Syriac makes glory the object — then will I sing to thee, Glory. With the pronoun the sense would be my heart; without it we must understand, with Jerome, renown or praise. John Gill takes it either of the soul, the nobler part, or of the tongue, which is the body’s glory and with which he glorified God. C.H. Spurgeon takes the same two options and draws the duty out: it would be a shameful crime if after receiving God’s mercies we forgot to praise him, and God would have no dumb children in his house — they are all to sing in heaven, and therefore should all sing on earth.

Adam Clarke rejects the anatomical guesses. The term is sometimes taken to signify the liver, and here is supposed to mean the tongue — why not the heart, he asks — but he thinks David means the state of exaltation and honour to which God had raised him, and in which he had before trusted too much. Now he has been disciplined into a better sentiment. My glory before had sung praise to myself, Clarke has him say; in it I rested, on it I presumed, and intoxicated with my success I sent Joab to number the people. Now that glory shall give thanks to God and never be silent, and I shall confess to all the world that the good and greatness and honour I possess came from God alone. He closes with the Old Psalter’s rendering in the old northern English, which turns the death and sorrow of our sin into the joy of remission and surrounds us at our dying with gladness, so that our joy may sing to him who gave it, since we are no longer stung with conscience of sin nor dread of death or doom.
